paragraphs.text: THE TWO LETTERS OF CLAUDIANUS MAMERTUS. THE FIRST LETTER.

If it were possible for me to meet you, my lord, even now and then and for a little while, I would not go asking about here and there into the wishes or needs of this person or that. I would ask only about the things that could be of use to me in the matter of what is owed me. The chance to visit is cut off in many ways, and for reasons just as wretched. And the means of writing is seldom available when it suits, or not available at all. Whether these things are pardonable or not, you yourself shall judge. Moreover, others are often favoured with your letters, though they do not seek them as I do and perhaps do not deserve them any more than I. This, I think, cannot be done with impunity under the laws of friendship. And must I still keep a painful silence about this too: that you have never favoured with a reply those books which you do not refuse to have ennobled by your name? But perhaps you have no spare time to spend even a little on a very great friendship. Yet what occupation could ever entangle you, anywhere, that does not turn to the benefit of others? When you appease God by prayer, you win his favour not only for your friends but for strangers as well. When you search out the mysteries of the heavenly Scriptures, the more eagerly you steep yourself in them, the more abundantly you pour learning out on others. When you lavish your wealth on the needs of the poor, you provide most of all for yourself, but for others too. So plainly there is nothing, absolutely nothing, among all your actions so barren that it bears fruit for you alone and does not yield a richer harvest for many others along with you. No pretext of any hindrance, then, can be offered, even falsely, why I, your particular and intimate friend, should gather no fruit from my particular friend, from whom a great many strangers gain so much. But I suppose that, after the pattern of the giver in the Gospel, what you do not give to a hungry friend you will give to a shameless knocker. And if you go on being as hard as usual, I will do something you will regret: if you sin further by keeping silent, I will at once take my revenge by writing. For there is no doubt that you will be punished by my writing just as much as I am punished by your silence. Farewell.

You declare, my elder lord, that the rights of close friendship are violated, because I have long held back from stylus and tablets where the greeting I owe you is concerned, and because for some time now my paper has burdened no traveller's hands with a letter honouring you with dutiful wishes for your health. You judge unfairly if you think that any mortal, at least any who cares to converse in Latin, does not tremble when he is brought as a writer to be examined by your ears. Your ears, I say: for unless the privilege of the ages that have run down to our own overawed me, I would not set even the stream of Fronto's gravity or of Apuleius' weight beside their expertise. Set beside them, the Varros, Atacinus and Terentius, and the Plinys, both the uncle and Secundus, would now look rustic. My judgment is confirmed by the volume on the state of the soul that you published, you who are richest in the knowledge of things and of words. Since you addressed its preface to me, I received from it this gift above all: the fame of my person, which did not deserve to grow illustrious through the titles of its own books, would be made lasting by the kindness of yours. But, great God, what a work that is, and how great! Its subject is locked up, its declamation is brilliant, its propositions bar the way, its argument opens the door; and though it is thorny with the barbed points of its syllogisms, it is honeyed with the flower of a springlike eloquence. Its words are new because they are old, and beside them even the style of ancient literature might rightly seem old-fashioned. What is more precious still, the whole diction is cut into clauses so concisely and yet flows so freely that you feel it, ample in matter and tight in its sentences, to teach more than it says. Indeed, this was once rightly reckoned the highest eloquence: to compress much into few words and to take care to fill out the case rather than the page. And what of this in your books: that a sustained maturity still admits tenderness, and severity weaves in a timely sweetness? So the reader's attention, wearied by passing through the sifted members of the philosophical disciplines, is suddenly refreshed by delightful digressions, as if in harbours of its own sea. O book powerful in many ways! O eloquence of a mind not meagre but subtle, which neither swells with hyperbolic gushings nor thins out into low abasement! Add to this a unique and singular learning, able to prove its case in the most varied matters. Its custom is to philosophize about each art with each of its masters. If chance requires, it does not refuse to hold the plectrum with Orpheus, the staff with Aesculapius, the rod with Archimedes, the horoscope with Euphrates, the compass with Perdix, the plumb line with Vitruvius. It has never ceased to investigate times with Thales, stars with Atlas, weights with Zethus, numbers with Chrysippus, measures with Euclid. In short, no one in my age has had such power to establish what he wished. When the work rises up against the man it argues against, it rightly claims for itself a share in the manners and studies of both languages. It thinks like Pythagoras, divides like Socrates, explains like Plato, entangles like Aristotle; it flatters like Aeschines, rages like Demosthenes, blossoms like Hortensius, burns like Cethegus, incites like Curio, delays like Fabius, feigns like Crassus, dissembles like Caesar, advises like Cato, dissuades like Appius, persuades like Tullius. And if we turn to the holy fathers for comparison, it instructs like Jerome, demolishes like Lactantius, builds up like Augustine, soars like Hilary, stoops like John, rebukes like Basil, consoles like Gregory, flows richly like Orosius, is concise like Rufinus, narrates like Eusebius, appeals like Eucherius, challenges like Paulinus, perseveres like Ambrose.

Now, if you ask what I think of your hymn: it is built of short clauses, and it is rich, sweet and lofty. It surpasses any lyric dithyramb in poetic charm and in historical truth. What is peculiar to you in it is this: while you observe the feet of the metres, the syllables of the feet and the quantities of the syllables, the poor verse encloses rich words within the bounds of its space, and the brevity of the constricted song does not shut out the length of ornate language. So it is easy for you to add to tiny trochees and tinier pyrrhics not only three-syllable molossi and anapaests but even four-syllable combinations of epitrites and paeons. The fullness of the expression outgrows the narrow limits of the rules. Like a great gem scarcely held by a small setting of gold, it flashes out like the spirit of a powerful horse: if he is held by the law of the bridle among wastes and broken ground as he chafes, you understand that what he lacks is not speed but a field to run in. Why say more? In my judgment, in both kinds of composition neither Athens will be judged so Attic nor the Muses so musical, provided long idleness has not taken from me even the ability to judge. For while, under cover of the profession thrust upon me, I am gradually taking up a new manner of writing and unlearning the old by leaps, nothing is left to me of the good orator except that I have more and more become a bad poet. So I beg you to pardon me this fault: though I remember you all the while, I only rarely mingle my drying little vein with your river. Your trumpet will rightly be revered as far as the whole world extends, for it is agreed that it sounded with a double good fortune: it found neither rival nor equal when, long ago, it travelled through the ears and mouths of the peoples, and I too helped to carry it about. For us, though, it is great audacity even to chatter before municipal orators and professors of the chair, or the wranglers of the forum, who, even while they plead (saving the honour of their betters), make up a large crowd devoting itself to the most unlettered of letters. As for you, who can thunder in both forms, as you please to alternate free prose and bound verse, few will imitate you, few "whom just Jupiter has loved." Farewell.
Claudianus to the most learned Sapaudus, rhetorician.

Greece, the mistress of all disciplines and arts, advanced so far in the noblest studies and embraced almost the whole world with her manifold learning chiefly for this reason: there was no one at all there who produced anything of good fruit without receiving an honour equal to his merit. Hence some mortals, almost surpassing mortal nature, stretched the powers of their excellent minds in every direction and searched out the hidden things of nature with untiring care. By investigation and art they grasped the stored-up causes of the first principles and the limits fixed for all time to substances that flow through time, and they entered not only the secret of the world but even what lies above the heavens.

I have occasion to say this now because the good arts have been lost ever since the age of our great-grandfathers. The human race spurns the cultivation of the mind, by which alone it excels the beasts, and serves luxury and riches as a handmaid of sloth and ignorance; so it has brought virtue to ruin along with learning. Apart from you alone, no one aspires to noble learning, not to bring anything new to it, nor even so far as to have something to unlearn. Shall we put that down to human negligence or to nature? If we blame this evil on a defect of nature, can the human race be said to differ from the human race? Are minds not the same as they were before? Did Cicero, the greatest orator of his age, count the gifts he was born with as enough? Did he not rather set little value on what home and city offered, and travel all the way to Greece to acquire a richer knowledge? Or was Plato, the peak and summit of philosophy, content with nature's private gift? After the teachings of Socrates, believing Greece too narrow in learning for the reach of his own virtues, did he not travel, a tireless searcher into things, to Egypt, and as far as the Brahmans of India, and as far as the heirs of the Pythagorean teachings? I pass over the others, since neither the time nor this work has room for it. This one thing I would say beyond doubt: in our age it is not talent that is lacking but study. I would bury these studies with a mournful epitaph, as though they were dead, had you not revived them by that same venerable profession, with praiseworthy skill, keen intelligence and flowing eloquence. This good thing is all the more admirable to me for having seemed so hopeless.

For I see that the Roman tongue is to the Romans not only a thing neglected but a thing to be ashamed of. Grammar, like some barbarian woman, is driven off with the fists and heels of barbarism and solecism. Dialectic is dreaded like an Amazon about to fight with drawn sword. Rhetoric, like a great lady, finds no welcome in narrow quarters. Music, geometry and arithmetic are spat upon like three Furies, and after them philosophy is counted as some ill-omened beast. But all this furnishes matter for your praise. If many shared your studies, you would of course be, if not the foremost of all, then one of many. As it is, with no injury to anyone else, in our Gaul you alone, and you only, are equal to your profession; and let this not be taken as flattery or fawning. I certainly cannot flatter, nor do you need false praise. But the sweetness of your declamations, mingled with strength, cannot be uprooted and torn from my mind. It is like Attic honey, whose very nature holds healing, strength and sweetness. On the ridges of Hybla the little bee, winged craftswoman, drinks in what falls from heaven, chews it and pours it into the flowery cells she has skilfully built; and, a maker of children from her own virginity, she nourishes her offspring and fills them with the rich abundance of the combs. So you, plucking from the greatest authors as from great mountains whatever is most learned, like fragrant thyme, and whatever is most fruitful, like flowers, fill them with the honey of your talent and make combs of eloquence. From these, likewise, a beloved multitude of pupils is formed for you, like children. Steeped also in the nectar of Greek learning, as if fed on Attic honey, once it begins to buzz on the wings of knowledge it too will make combs of eloquence. Only be sure to remember that the office of teaching has come down to you as an inheritance from your great-grandfathers onward. So you must strive all the harder after knowledge, since the manifold learning of your ancestors has flowed together in you.

You must also be reminded of the ancient nobility of the city of Vienne, whose citizen and teacher you are. You will not pay your double debt by idleness, since you are required in two ways to answer both to your fathers and to your fatherland. Last of all, at the end of this letter, I ask you as a close friend to scorn the childish trifles of newfangled little arguments. Spend no time reading the works that crack the rattling of resounding little phrases like whips, and unman the strength of oratory with applauding jingles. Let Naevius and Plautus serve you for acquiring elegance, Cato for gravity, Varro for learning, Gracchus for sharpness, Chrysippus for discipline, Fronto for grandeur, Cicero for eloquence. For whoever among more recent writers has written anything worthy of memory did not himself read the moderns. So the writers to be gone over again and committed to memory are those from whom the men we admire were able to profit. I have perhaps offered this testimony of friendship a little too familiarly, but your goodwill will grant pardon to the boldness of love.
